catalog_quote: Stress and intonation. The lexical tone contrast from the Central Franconian tonal accents (Gussenhoven & Peters 2004) has completely disappeared from Luxembourgish (Gilles 2002). ... Word accent in Luxembourgish may fall on the antepenultimate, the penultimate or the final syllable, with the penult as the most common stress pattern, which frequently also applies to French loans like Parfum [ˈpɑχ f ː] ‘fragrant’, Dekolleté [deːˈkolteː] ‘décolleté’. Although schwa syllables normally avoid word stress (Atelier [ˈɑtəljeː] ‘workshop’), disyllabic words with an initial schwa syllable nevertheless can attract word stress (Tëlee [ˈtəleː] ‘television’) (Gilles 2009). Little is known yet about intonation, but a typical intonational feature of Luxembourgish is the rising-mid-falling nuclear tune, which serves to signal continuation. ... sweep_summary: Six title-hit items for luxe1241; none is a word-stress source for Luxembourgish. Rispail & Moreau 2004 (Glottopol 4) was downloaded open and read: sociolinguistic recognition of regional accents, silent on word stress. Gilles 2002 (tonal accent, paywalled DOI; ORBilu 'No full text'), Gilles 2006 (n-deletion/Eifel rule, print-only) and Goudaillier 1989 (F0 synthesis of the Schärfung tonal accent, print-only) are prosody-but-not-word-stress. Jongen 1972 describes the Moresnet dialect, which is Platdiets (East Limburgish–Ripuarian transitional, Plombières municipality), a different variety; no open copy. Schanen 2006 'Prosodie luxembourgeoise' (Festschrift Kohnen) is unclear and print-only — medium priority. The best stress statement read is Gilles 2023 ORE p.12 (held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass): penult default, heavy final attracts stress, open finals never stressed, schwa penults stressable — a refinement of the catalog's 'lexical' coding toward a weight-conditioned right-edge system; the primary Gilles 2009 Wortakzent paper (ORBilu 10993/3327, restricted) is still the top acquisition target though not in this item list.

new_statements.quote: Word stress is usually on the penultimate syllable (Gilles, 2009). With most words consisting of two syllables, the trochaic stress pattern is widespread. […] schwa syllables can also attract stress if they are in the penultimate position and no other stressable syllable is available (ˈfëschen [ˈfəʃən] 'to fish', ˈkënnen 'can (modal verb)'). In case the final syllable is heavy, this syllable will attract stress (Spiˈdol 'hospital', Taˈpéit 'wallpaper', Eleˈment 'element', aktuˈell 'current'). However, and in contrast to Standard German, open final syllables never carry stress

new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by the same first author as the catalog's deciding source, ten years later, formulated as a rule: default penultimate (trochaic) stress; a heavy final syllable attracts stress; open final syllables are never stressed (French loans shift final stress to the penult, or to the antepenult when the penult has schwa or a short high vowel); schwa penults can bear stress; compounds may stress the second constituent. This refines the catalog's JIPA quote ('antepenult, penult or final, penult most common'): the ORE describes a weight-conditioned right-edge system rather than free lexical placement, with antepenultimate stress arising only from penult-avoidance in loans. Gilles 2014 (held by the project, lines 360-361) agrees: 'Word stress.. falls in most cases on the penultimate syllable creating trochaic feet (cf. Gilles 2010)'. The dedicated primary source both texts cite, Gilles 2009/2010 'Wie Französisch, nur Ton 1 — Der Wortakzent des Deutschen und Luxemburgischen im Kontrast' (ORBilu 10993/3327, restricted), remains unobtained. This file was downloaded in the 2026-09-16 pass and re-read in this search of works with stress in the title (a copy we already held, read).

tone_statements.quote: Engelmann (1910: 383–385) impressionistically described the difference between Accent 1 and 2 (the weak and the strong template) in Moselle-Franconian of Vianden as follows. Under Accent 1, syllables end with a sudden loss of expiration, and under Accent 2, they fade slowly. Engelmann also observed laryngoscopically an overt glottal closure after a vowel or a coda sonorant in Accent 1, especially under strong sentence-final stress (cf. SM2). [...] responsible for all observed acoustic differences in vocalic and consonantal duration between the two accents, as well as for the voicing contrast of consonants (while the pitch curve appears the same under both accents in this variety).

sources.citation: Conrad, François. 2017. Schwa-Elision und die Wortprosodie des Luxemburgischen. Linguistik Online 80(1): 21-49. doi:10.13092/lo.80.3564
sources.quote: Nach Analyse der Sprachdaten aus dem Sprachexperiment ergab sich jedoch, dass im Lb. in allen untersuchten Wortarten die daktylische Form durch Ausfall des Schwa-Vokals in (deutlich) mehr als der Hälfte der Fälle von der trochäischen Form abgelöst wird. Durch Schwa-Elision verschiebt sich somit die prosodische Struktur zugunsten des Trochäus. Wie im Dt. herrscht der Trochäus im Lb. also vor. Anders als im Dt. treten jedoch zusätzlich weiterhin zahlreiche Daktylen auf.

sources.note: Empirical study (15 speakers) of schwa deletion after stressed syllables in Luxembourgish and its effect on word-prosodic foot structure, finding a shift from dactyl toward the trochee as the unmarked foot type.
